And the Key Biodiversity Areas program has made progress in strengthening its monitoring framework to do the same. Further, the Panorama Platform, a multi-stakeholder knowledge management initiative, identifies and promotes examples of tested and replicable solutions in biodiversity conservation, land management, and sustainable development more broadly. Distinguished delegates, On behalf of civil society and indigenous peoples, we welcome the report on knowledge sharing, technology transfer and innovation, and commend the Secretariat, the SPI, WOCAT and partners for their efforts. It is important to recognize that without dedicated, predictable financing and formal mechanisms for civil society and community participation, these tools risk remaining inaccessible to those who need them the most. We therefore like to highlight the following key aspects. First, knowledge sharing must be inclusive and participatory. CSOs, indigenous peoples, local communities, pastoralists, women and youth have to participate meaningfully in generating, sharing and applying knowledge. Second, traditional, local and indigenous knowledge must be recognized alongside scientific knowledge. Community knowledge should be systematically integrated into knowledge platforms, technology transfer initiatives, scientific assessments and capacity building. Third, knowledge data and technologies must be openly accessible. Scientific information, data sets, methodologies, and tools should be available through multilingual user-friendly systems. Fourth, technology transfer must empower local actors for them to access, adapt, and apply technologies through capacity building and peer-to-peer learning. Fifth, community-led innovation must be recognized and scaled up. This includes evidence-based agroecological approaches, regional restoration, participatory water management, and community-based monitoring. Sixth, innovation should support integrated and resilient land systems. This could help to strengthen synergies across the Rio Conventions and address interconnected environmental changes. Finally, digital technologies and artificial intelligence must complement, not replace, community knowledge, local expertise and participatory decision-making. Clear ethical guidelines, data protection standards, and indigenous data sovereignty principles must govern the design and deployment of AI tools. Distinguished delegates, the success of knowledge sharing, technology transfer, and innovation will ultimately depend on whether they reach and empower those restoring land, managing water, and building resilience every day. We call to parties to adopt concrete time-bound decision at COP17 that translate these priorities into resources action. Thank you.

Thank you, Chair. Distinguished delegates, I have the honour to introduce document ICCD/COP17/CS-T/5, which corresponds to draft decision four in document ICCD/COP17/CST/8. Document CST/5 is entitled Preparations for the Future Functioning of the Science-Policy Interface. By its decision 20/COP16, the Conference of the Parties requested the development during the 2025-2026 transition biennium of a number of elements needed for the future functioning of the science policy interface, beginning with the 2027-2030 quadrennium, covering membership and governance, procedures for requests and outputs, technical support, cooperation with other intergovernmental science policy bodies, and financial implications. In response, the Bureau of Committee on Science and Technology, with the support of the Secretariat, and input from the SPI undertook work during the 2025-2026 biennium to prepare the institutional, procedural and operational foundations for the future functioning of the SPI. This included the renewal of SPI membership for the transition biennium, preparations for the transition for four-year work programmes, the development and training of new procedures, consideration of cooperation with partner scientific bodies, and the preparation of feasibility study on technical support arrangements, including the possible use of an external technical support unit. I am joined on the podium by the UNCCD Chief Scientist who will present the work summarised in the document CST/5. Thank you, Chair.

Thank you, Chair. Brazil recalls that paragraph six of the decision 20/COP16 requested the CST Bureau to develop and submit for the consideration of the CST at its 17th session, procedures for receiving and prioritizing requests to the SPI for the preparation of flagship reports and for fast-track assessments, information products, and advice. In this regard, we therefore understand that these procedures are before us at this session for substantive consideration and agreement by parties, and we highlight the importance of discussing the document ICCD/COP17/CST/5 in the contact group. Brazil appreciates the extensive work undertaken by the Bureau, the Secretariat and the SPI. Our concern is to ensure a clear distinction between the important role of the Bureau in facilitating and preparing intersessional work and the role of the CST as the intergovernmental body in taking substantive decisions and approving outputs that are to carry intergovernmental authority. In this regard, Brazil would like to highlight three specific issues. First, Regarding the summary for policymakers, the current procedures are not fully consistent in this respect. Table 3 states under how parties shape flagship reports that parties participate through CST consideration and approval of the recommendations in the SPMs by consensus. by way of discussions of the flagship report document and the corresponding draft decision. The projected GLO4 timeline on page 12 similarly envisages the SPM recommendations being translated into a draft CST decision for approval. Brazil believes that approval only of the recommendations is not sufficient. The summary for policymakers itself in its entirety should be subject to intergovernmental line by line consideration and approval by parties through the SCT prior to publication. This is important because the SPM as a whole, its findings, key messages, framing, and policy-oriented recommendations is the principal policy-facing product of the assessment. Intergovernmental authorities should therefore attach to the SPM as a whole rather than only to recommendations subsequently incorporated into a CST decision. This is also consistent with established practice under both the IPCC and the IPBES where the SPM itself is subject to line by line consideration and approval by their respective intergovernmental bodies. We note that other language already introduced in table 3 moves precisely in this direction, referring to the SPM being considered and approved through an intergovernmental line-by-line review by Parties prior to publication, and to the SPM itself being subject to line-by-line discussion and agreement. We support this approach and believe that the entire Table 3 as well as the GLO-4 timeline should be made consistent with it. Second, regarding the topic of GLO-4 and the SPI work programme, the general procedure in Table 2 provides that the Bureau prepares recommendations on the SPI work programme that are subsequently transmitted to Parties for consideration and decision. However, for the 2027-2030 quadriennium, an exception is proposed under which approval of the topic of the GLO4 and the update of the SPI work programme would be undertaken by the CST Bureau. We understand that this exception has been proposed because of the particular time constraints associated with the first quadriennial cycle. Nevertheless, approval of the topic of a flagship report and of the SPI work programme is a substantive decision that should remain with Parties through the CST. Brazil is therefore prepared to be flexible regarding the timeline for this first report, recognising the transitional nature of this cycle. If additional time is required, we could adjust the GLO4 timeline and explore practical solutions, including, if necessary, the possibility of an extraordinary session of the CST back-to-back with CRIC-25. Flexibility in the timetable would be preferable to transferring these substantive decisions to the Bureau. Third, regarding future changes to these procedures, Table 3 currently provides that the CST Bureau may periodically review and update these procedures. We agree that the Bureau should review implementation and identify possible improvements. However, if these procedures are now considered and agreed by Parties through the CST, they should not subsequently be substantively amended by the Bureau alone. We would therefore suggest that the Bureau may periodically review their implementation and propose updates for consideration and approval by the CST. The aforementioned edits to text should also be reflected in Table 1. Chair, our intention is not to limit the important role of the Bureau or the scientific independence of the SPI. Rather, A clear division of responsibilities strengthens both scientific credibility and intergovernmental legitimacy. The SPI should lead the scientific work, the Bureau should facilitate, coordinate and prepare intersessional work, and Parties through the CST should retain responsibility for substantive intergovernmental decision-making and approval. We therefore look forward to examining tables one, two and three, as well as the corresponding GLO4 timeline and relevant provisions of the draft decision in the contact group. Thank you, Chair.

I thank the distinguished representative of Zimbabwe. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of UNESCO.

I thank the distinguished representative of UNESCO. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative, civil society, British Society of Soil Science.

Thank you, Chair, distinguished delegates. On behalf of the civil society and indigenous peoples, we welcome progress in preparing the future functioning of the science policy interface. and commend the CST Bureau, the SPI and the Secretariat for laying the foundations for its 2027-2030 work programme. Under CST5, we welcome efforts to transition to quadrilateral functioning, strengthen procedures for scientific outputs, enhance technical support for SPI and cooperation with partner scientific bodies. However, The SPI future success will depend not only on scientific excellence, but also on being inclusive, transparent, accessible, interdisciplinary and responsive to communities affected by desertification, land degradation and drought. Civil society therefore highlights seven priorities. First, Meaningful participation must be embedded throughout the SPI's work. The whole of civil society must participate systematically in the scoping, development, review, dissemination and application of SPI outputs. Second, local communities and indigenous knowledge must be fully integrated alongside scientific evidence. Clear mechanisms are needed to incorporate knowledge from communities with generations of experience in sustainable land management. Third, community-generated evidence must be recognised. Community-based monitoring, citizen science, participatory data collection must be better integrated into scientific assessments and reporting. Fourth, scientific knowledge must be accessible and useful. SPI guidance and knowledge products should be available through open, multilingual and user-friendly platforms that reach policymakers, the private sector and the whole of civil society, including indigenous peoples. Fifth, strengthen interdisciplinary and system-based approaches, land degradation, droughts, biodiversity loss. Food insecurity, water scarcity, climate change and disaster risk reduction are interconnected. SPI work must strengthen synergies with the Rio Conventions and the Sendai Framework and advance land-based solutions with multiple environmental and social benefits. Sixth, invest in capacity building and knowledge exchange, particularly for grassroots organisations, civil society, women, youth, indigenous peoples and local communities. So SPI outputs can translate into global, national, regional and local implementation. Finally, strengthen gender responsive science and ensure adequate long term support. This requires gender expertise, gender disaggregated data and meaningful participation, including predictable resources. The SPI's establishment as a permanent mechanism is a significant achievement. Its future must combine scientific excellence with inclusion, accessibility and practical relevance. By connecting diverse knowledge systems with policy and action, the SPI can become an even stronger bridge between science and implementation, contributing to resilient landscapes equitable development and sustainable futures for all. Thank you, Chair.
